claims.text: Local atomic-scale disorder and surface strain heterogeneity govern the onset of premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles.
Higher surface disorder and strain cause liquid-like surface layers to form at lower temperatures.
As-synthesized HEA nanoparticles possess high configurational disorder.
The as-synthesized HEA nanoparticles have a uniform, single-phase alloy structure.
Rapid quenching produces greater surface disorder and strain than mild post-synthesis annealing.
Mild annealing reduces surface disorder, defect density, and strain.
In situ TEM can monitor nanoscale kinetic evolution at high spatial resolution.
Restricting the study to nanoparticles below approximately 10 nm accentuates surface effects relevant to premelting.
Local disorder and strain disrupt interatomic cohesive forces at the nanoparticle surface.
Disruption of surface cohesion causes earlier surface reconstruction and formation of a premelted liquid-like layer.
A premelted surface layer facilitates complete melting at a lower temperature than in structurally ordered nanoparticles.
Premelting onset temperature and layer extent correlate with measured surface defect density and strain.
Annealed nanoparticles with fewer surface defects have higher premelting and melting temperatures.
The proposed trend applies to HEA nanoparticles below 10 nm from several hundred degrees below their bulk melting point through complete melting.
HEA nanoparticles are relevant to catalysis, sensing, energy-related, and corrosion-related applications requiring stability.
The quantitative relationship between disorder or strain and premelting temperature may vary with subtle compositional differences.
Statistically equivalent premelting onset temperatures and extents despite confirmed disorder differences would falsify the proposed governing role of disorder and strain.
